rows.answer: When they signed up, the people who went on to keep 100-day streaks were mostly complete beginners, while a lot of the people in the other group had studied Spanish before. So the two groups didn't start from the same place, the comparison isn't fair, and you can't credit the streaks for the higher scores.
The letter is written on Holt paper.
Even though some members want the silo left exactly as it is, the writer's position is that the society ought not to stand in the way of converting it into apartments.

The ad gets cause and effect backwards. It assumes the users who already spoke Spanish better were the ones who kept 100-day streaks, when really it's keeping the streak that made them score higher on the speaking test.
